title: 3-Read Friday #79: Motivation, Working Memory, and Correct Answers Without Learning
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #79 links three posts united by a shared worry: that surface-level signals of success - motivational buzzwords, task completion, correct answers - can mask an absence of genuine learning underneath. Andrew Watson digs beneath the popular three-word summary of self-determination theory (autonomy, relatedness, competence) to show that individual motivational strategies can help one of these needs while undermining another, meaning teachers cannot simply apply the theory's headline advice as a formula. Mike Hobbiss builds a visual model of the brain's limited-capacity attention and working memory systems, showing how these two bottlenecks interact and what concrete teaching moves (reducing distraction, cueing attention, connecting to long-term memory) help work within those limits. Carl Hendrick uses a small, personal moment - watching his daughter complete a phonics puzzle by matching colours rather than blending sounds - to illustrate a much larger principle: tasks that produce correct answers through superficial pattern-matching can be worse than useless, because they actively train students to avoid the deeper cognitive processing the task was meant to build. Barton's framing draws the three together around a single caution: don't mistake fluency, motivation-talk, or correctness for evidence that real learning has occurred.
points: Andrew Watson's central caution about self-determination theory: strategies meant to build one of the 'big three' needs (autonomy, relatedness, competence) can simultaneously undermine another - e.g., offering a struggling student a hint can boost relatedness while reducing their sense of autonomy and competence.

Watson's broader methodological point: research-backed motivational strategies shouldn't be applied as a one-size-fits-all formula, but filtered through questions about individual differences, cultural context, and whether the strategy fits a specific student's actual needs.

Mike Hobbiss's visual model shows attention and working memory as sequential limited-capacity bottlenecks that reinforce each other - filling attention with task-relevant information is the main lever available, since capacity itself cannot be meaningfully trained up.

Hobbiss's key practical lever beyond attention and working memory: information already well-connected in long-term memory can be recalled as a single 'chunk,' dramatically expanding what students can effectively hold and manipulate in working memory.

Carl Hendrick's central story - his daughter completing a phonics puzzle via colour-matching rather than phoneme blending - illustrates that tasks producing correct answers through surface-level pattern matching can actively teach the wrong cognitive habit, what he calls 'expertise in superficiality.'
quotes: I love Andrew's research deep-dives. Here, he explores Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory, delving beyond the headlines to consider what this concept looks like in the classroom.
A super clear overview of the limitations of our brains in terms of attention and working memory capacity.
The illustrations are especially useful and could be shared with students to help them better understand how they learn.
